newsitem.title: USA: WJC assails Swiss President for remarks.
newsitem.headline: WJC assails Swiss President for remarks.

text.p: Swiss President Jean-Pascal Delamuraz had shown "shocking insensitivity" by suggesting Jews had resorted to "blackmail" in seeking compensation for money left in Swiss banks as a safe haven from Nazi looting, the World Jewish Congress said on Tuesday.

The group, which along with U.S. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Alfonse D'Amato has demanded Switzerland establish a compensation fund for Holocaust survivors and their heirs who might be entitled to money left in Swiss banks, said Delamuraz's reported comments present "an assault and challenge to the very soul of Switzerland."

In a newspaper interview, Delamuraz on Tuesday dismissed the calls for the fund as "blackmail" and accused foreign critics of trying to undermine Switzerland's role as a world financial centre with charges the Swiss profited cynically from the Second World War.

"He has shown shocking insensitivity to the moral concerns of the Jewish people as well as others who feel deeply the tragedy of the Holocaust and those terrible years," World Jewish Congress (WJC) vice-president Kalman Sultanik said in a statement in New York. "I do not believe the Swiss people will allow this blackening of the reputation of their country."

In some of the strongest language used so far by Swiss politicians, Delamuraz rejected the creation of a $250 million fund he said had been proposed to special ambassador Thomas Borer, who met critics from the WJC and Sen. D'Amato in December.

"This is nothing less than extortion and blackmail. This fund would make it much more difficult to establish the truth," Delamuraz told the French-language Swiss newspaper Tribune de Geneve. "Such a fund would be considered an admission of guilt."

Delamuraz repeated the Swiss government's stance that any compensation measures should wait for the findings of a nine-member historical panel named by the Cabinet two weeks ago to investigate the Swiss financial role in the Second World War.
